(1) the edge arrival rate, and not the node arrival rate, determines the growth rate of the network; and (2) the gap process, and not the triangle closing process, is responsible for the power law distribution of out degree in the network.

(i) edge locality plays a dominant role in evolution of social networks, and (ii) the combination of a triangle closing edge selection model with node lifetimes results in power law out degree distributions.
the evolution of social networks is characterized by two distinct processes: node arrivals and the creation of edges between nodes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of social networks, and the development of a new model of network formation based on a simple triangle closing process.
the microscopic processes that underlie the formation and evolution of large online social networks.
the evolution of social networks from a microscopic point of view.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the network formation process is not as random as previously thought, and is instead highly localized.
the evolution of social networks is driven by a combination of node arrival and edge formation, with the latter being a local process.
the observed network evolution can be explained by a simple model of node arrival and edge initiation, where the node arrival rate is the only parameter that needs to be adjusted to fit the data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the microscopic evolution of social networks is dominated by a combination of edge locality and preferential attachment.
a simple model of edge formation based on local triangle closing can generate a realistic network, given the arrival and lifetime of nodes.
we provide the first microscopic description of network evolution and the most accurate model for generating realistic synthetic networks.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the macroscopic properties of a social network are the result of a combination of microscopic processes, and the interplay between them.
a combination of a few basic processes can lead to a realistic evolution of large scale online social networks, with a wide range of macroscopic properties.
the microscopic details of the network evolution process are crucial in understanding the macroscopic network structure.
